To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

we have identified two germline genetic variants that predispose to myeloproliferaive neoplasms, and that these variants are more common in patients who carry mutations in CALR and MPL than in those with the JAK2V6F17 mutation, suggesting that the germline genetic risk is more important in the former two subtypes.
germline variants in the MECOM, HBS1L, MYB, JAK2, and TERT genes predispose to MPNs.
germline variants in MECOM, JAK2, TERT, HBS1L/MYP and other genes predispose to myeloproliterative neoplasims (MPN).
In summary, our research is concerned with
the genetic and molecular mechanisms of myeloproliferation and the development of MPN.
the role of germline genetic variation in predisposition to myeloprolifieration neoplasms.
the identification of genetic variants associated with MPN.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the risk for MPN in the general population is increased by a genetic variation at MECOMECOM (also known as EVI1), TERT, J2AK and HBS1LMYB.
the risk of MPNs is influenced by genetic variation in the JAK2, TERT, MECOM, JAK2, and HBS1-MYB genes.
the germline variants in the JAK2, MECOM, MYB, HBS1L/MYC, TERT, and JAK2 regions are not associated with MPN, but with the risk of developing MPN.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
germline genetic variation in JAK2 and MECOM, as well as TERT and HBS1l/MYB, predisposes to myeloid clonal proliferation.
the genetic variants identified are not sufficient to cause MPN but rather increase the likelihood of developing the disease.
germline variation in MECOM, HBS1L/MYC and TERT predisposes to myeloid neoplasia, but that the effect of these variants is modified by JAK2V616F, CALR or other mutations.
The main takeaway from our work is that
there are germline genetic factors that contribute to MPN development and these factors are different in the three main MPN subtypes.
there are germline variants in the genome that predispose to the development of MPNs.
genetic factors play an important role in the pathogenesis of myeloproliferation, which may be independent of somatic driver mutations.
